Acknowledge
ac-knŏl´edge
v. (to own, confess, or recognize; rendering Hebrew yada, nakar, Greek homologeo, epiginosko)
From ac- (to) and knowledge — to bring a thing into the open as known. In Scripture acknowledgment is knowledge that has been owned, and owning it usually costs something.

Biblical Definition

Acknowledge is knowledge admitted aloud, and Scripture uses it for the two hardest admissions a man makes. The first is his own sin: “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid… and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin” (Psa 32:5) — the acknowledging and the forgiving in one verse, with nothing between them. David repeats it in the great penitential psalm: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me” (Psa 51:3). Judah supplies the Old Testament's starkest instance, publicly owning both the pledge and the verdict: “Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I” (Gen 38:26). The second admission is God's right to direct a life: “In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths” (Pro 3:6) — not consult Him at the crossroads, but acknowledge Him in all the ways, which is why the promise of direction follows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines acknowledge as to own, avow or admit to be true, by a declaration of assent — and to own or confess, as in relation to a fault or crime.

expand to see more

ACKNOWL´EDGE, v.t. To own, avow or admit to be true, by a declaration of assent; as to acknowledge the being of a God.

2. To own or notice with particular regard.

In all thy ways acknowledge him. Prov. iii.

3. To own or confess, as in relation to a fault or crime. 4. To own with gratitude; as, to acknowledge a favor.

Key Scripture

Psa 32:5 — "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah."

Pro 3:6 — "In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

Gen 38:26 — "And Judah acknowledged them, and said, She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son. And he knew her again no more."

Psa 51:3 — "For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me."

Modern Corruption

Confession replaced by explanation — the account of oneself that acknowledges circumstances, upbringing, or misunderstanding, but never the sin — and guidance sought at crossroads by men who acknowledge God nowhere else.

expand to see more

The modern apology is a masterpiece of evasion: regret for how something was received, acknowledgment of impact, sorrow that offence was taken. Psalm 32:5 has a different grammar. I acknowledged my sin… mine iniquity have I not hid. The object of the verb is the sin itself, owned as the speaker's own, without a modifying clause. And the forgiveness follows immediately in the same sentence, which is the most encouraging thing about the verse — there is no waiting period between the honest admission and the pardon.

Proverbs 3:6 is the other correction, and it is routinely miscited. It is quoted as a decision-making formula: bring God the big choices and He will show you which way to go. But the text says in all thy ways, and the promise of direction is attached to that comprehensiveness. A man who acknowledges God in his work, his speech, his marriage, and his money is generally not agonizing over guidance, because the direction has been given continuously. Guidance is the fruit of an acknowledged Lordship, not a service offered to strangers.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yada (H3045), to know, and in acknowledgment to know openly; nakar (H5234), to recognize, discern — Judah recognizing his own pledge; Greek homologeo (G3670), to say the same thing.

expand to see more

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know, acknowledge; the verb of Pro 3:6, knowing God in all one's ways.

Hebrew nakar (H5234) — to recognize, acknowledge; Judah acknowledging his signet, bracelets, and staff (Gen 38:26).

Greek homologeo (G3670) — to speak the same thing, agree, confess; confession is agreeing with God's verdict rather than offering one's own (1Jn 1:9).

Usage

"“I acknowledged my sin unto thee… and thou forgavest” — nothing stands between the two clauses."

"“In all thy ways acknowledge him” — guidance is the fruit of comprehensive Lordship."

"“She hath been more righteous than I” — Judah owns the pledge and the verdict together."
